title: LES FÉES
work: Histoires ou contes du temps passé
source: Charles Perrault, « LES FÉES », dans Histoires ou contes du temps passé. Avec des Moralitez (Paris, Claude Barbin, 1697) ; texte de l’édition originale d’après la transcription de Wikisource, orthographe de 1697 conservée. Prononciation : français standard moderne ; les graphies de 1697 sont lues selon l’usage moderne.
about: «Les Fées» is a tale built on a single contrast: a widow’s two daughters, one gentle and one proud, each meet a fairy at a spring, and each receives a gift that matches her manners, so that one speaks flowers and precious stones and the other snakes and toads. The word to watch is «honnesteté», which in 1697 meant courtesy and good breeding rather than honesty; the notes follow it, and its opposite, through the tale. The book closes the story with two short verse morals, printed here as part of the text.

sentences.t: Il estoit une fois une Veuve qui avoit deux filles :
sentences.say: Il était une fois une Veuve qui avait deux filles :
sentences.l: There was one time a widow who had two daughters:
sentences.i: Once upon a time there was a widow who had two daughters.
sentences.n: «Il estoit une fois» is the storyteller’s fixed opening: «il» is the impersonal ‘it’, standing where English says ‘there’, «estoit» is the 1697 spelling of «était» ‘was’, and «une fois» is ‘one time, once’. Lectorium gives it the matching English formula, ‘once upon a time’, in every tale it opens (Cendrillon prints it «Il eſtoit», with the long s). «avoit» is «avait» ‘had’, the same 1697 imperfect in «-oit»; the capital on «Veuve» ‘widow’ is the printer’s, as on many common nouns in this book.

sentences.t: l’aisnée luy ressembloit si fort d’humeur et de visage, que qui la voyoit, voyoit la mere.
sentences.say: l’aînée lui ressemblait si fort d’humeur et de visage, que qui la voyait, voyait la mère.
sentences.l: the elder resembled her so strongly in humour and in face, that whoever saw her, saw the mother.
sentences.i: the elder was so like her in temper and in looks that whoever saw the daughter saw the mother.
sentences.n: «l’aisnée» is «l’aînée» ‘the elder (daughter)’, and «luy» is «lui» ‘(to) her’: 1697 writes an s before a consonant where modern French has a circumflex, and y where it has i. «humeur» is ‘temper, disposition’, the old sense of English ‘humour’. In «qui la voyoit, voyoit la mere», «qui» with nothing before it means ‘whoever’; «voyoit» is «voyait», and «mere» is «mère», printed without its accent.

sentences.t: Elles estoient toutes deux si desagreables et si orgueilleuses, qu’on ne pouvoit vivre avec elles.
sentences.say: Elles étaient toutes deux si désagréables et si orgueilleuses, qu’on ne pouvait vivre avec elles.
sentences.l: They were both of them so disagreeable and so proud, that one could not live with them.
sentences.i: Both were so disagreeable and so proud that no one could live with them.
sentences.n: «si … que» is ‘so … that’. «ne pouvoit» without «pas» is ‘could not’: with «pouvoir» the «pas» could be, and in careful writing still can be, left out. «desagreables» is «désagréables» without its accents.

sentences.t: La Cadette, qui estoit le vray portrait de son pere pour la douceur et l’honnesteté, estoit avec cela une des plus belles filles qu’on eust su voir.
sentences.say: La Cadette, qui était le vrai portrait de son père pour la douceur et l’honnêteté, était avec cela une des plus belles filles qu’on eût su voir.
sentences.l: The younger, who was the true portrait of her father for gentleness and courtesy, was with that one of the most beautiful girls that one could have seen.
sentences.i: The younger, the very image of her father in gentleness and courtesy, was besides one of the most beautiful girls ever seen.
sentences.n: «la Cadette» is ‘the younger daughter’. «honnesteté» (modern «honnêteté») is not ‘honesty’ here: in 1697 it is the courtesy and decent good manners of a well-bred person, and the tale turns on it, so the English says ‘courtesy’ throughout. «vray» is «vrai» ‘true’, and «avec cela» ‘with that’ is ‘besides, into the bargain’. «eust» is «eût», the imperfect subjunctive of «avoir», a tense of elevated written French; with «su» ‘been able’ it forms the pluperfect subjunctive, which here has the force of ‘could have’, so after the superlative «qu’on eust su voir» is ‘that one could ever have seen’.

sentences.t: Comme on aime naturellement son semblable, cette mere estoit folle de sa fille aisnée, et en même temps avoit une aversion effroyable pour la Cadette.
sentences.say: Comme on aime naturellement son semblable, cette mère était folle de sa fille aînée, et en même temps avait une aversion effroyable pour la Cadette.
sentences.l: As one loves naturally one’s like, this mother was mad about her elder daughter, and at the same time had a frightful aversion for the younger.
sentences.i: Since like naturally loves like, the mother doted on her elder daughter, and at the same time had a dreadful loathing for the younger.
sentences.n: «son semblable» is ‘one’s like, whoever resembles one’, so the opening clause is the proverb that like loves like. «estre folle de» ‘to be mad about’ is ‘to dote on’. «même» already has its modern circumflex here, though the book elsewhere prints «mesme»: spelling was not yet fixed.

sentences.t: Elle la faisoit manger à la Cuisine & travailler sans cesse.
sentences.say: Elle la faisait manger à la Cuisine et travailler sans cesse.
sentences.l: She made her eat in the kitchen and work without ceasing.
sentences.i: She made her eat in the kitchen and work without rest.
sentences.n: «faire» with an infinitive is ‘to make (someone) do’: «la faisoit manger» ‘made her eat’. «&» is the printer’s sign for «et» ‘and’. To eat in the kitchen was to eat with the servants, not at the family’s table.

sentences.t: Il falloit entre-autre chose que cette pauvre enfant allast deux fois le jour puiser de l’eau à une grande demy lieue du logis, & qu’elle en raportast plein une grande cruche.
sentences.say: Il fallait entre-autre chose que cette pauvre enfant allât deux fois le jour puiser de l’eau à une grande demi lieue du logis, et qu’elle en rapportât plein une grande cruche.
sentences.l: It was needful among other things that this poor child should go two times a day to draw water at a long half-league from the house, and that she should bring back a big pitcher full of it.
sentences.i: Among other things, the poor child had to go twice a day to draw water a good half-league from the house, and bring back a large pitcher full.
sentences.n: «il falloit que» (modern «il fallait que») ‘it was needful that’ takes the subjunctive, here the imperfect subjunctive again: «allast» and «raportast» are «allât» and «rapportât» in the 1697 spelling. «entre-autre chose» is ‘among other things’, and «puiser» is ‘to draw (water)’. A league was a measure of road distance, roughly two and a half to three miles, so «une grande demy lieue» ‘a long half-league’ is well over a mile each way; «demy» is «demi». «logis» is ‘dwelling, house’.

sentences.t: Un jour qu’elle estoit à cette fontaine, il vint à elle une pauvre femme qui la pria de luy donner à boire ?
sentences.say: Un jour qu’elle était à cette fontaine, il vint à elle une pauvre femme qui la pria de lui donner à boire ?
sentences.l: One day that she was at this spring, there came to her a poor woman who begged her to give her [something] to drink.
sentences.i: One day, when she was at the spring, a poor woman came up to her and begged her for a drink.
sentences.n: «fontaine» here is a spring, where water rises from the ground, not an ornamental fountain. «il vint» ‘there came’ is the passé simple of «venir», and «pria» ‘begged, asked’ that of «prier»: the passé simple is the elevated narrative tense of the written tale, used for events told one after another, while the imperfect in «-oit» sets the scene. «donner à boire» ‘to give to drink’ needs no object in French, and the literal line supplies [something]. The request is reported, not asked, yet the witness ends the sentence with a question mark; Lectorium prints its witness unaltered, and the English gives a plain statement.

sentences.t: Ouy da, ma bonne mere, dit cette belle fille,
sentences.say: Oui da, ma bonne mère, dit cette belle fille,
sentences.l: Yes indeed, my good mother, said this beautiful girl,
sentences.i: Why, yes, good mother, said the beautiful girl,
sentences.n: «Ouy da» (modern «oui-da») is a warm, familiar ‘yes indeed, gladly’. «ma bonne mere» ‘my good mother’ is a kindly way to address an old woman of the common people, not a claim of kinship. «dit» ‘said’ is the passé simple, set inside the speech as its tag.

sentences.t: & rainçant aussi-tost sa cruche, elle puisa de l’eau au plus belle endroit de la fontaine, & la lui presenta, soûtenant toûjours la cruche afin qu’elle bût plus aisément.
sentences.say: et rinçant aussitôt sa cruche, elle puisa de l’eau au plus belle endroit de la fontaine, et la lui présenta, soutenant toujours la cruche afin qu’elle bût plus aisément.
sentences.l: and rinsing at once her pitcher, she drew some water at the most beautiful spot of the spring, and presented it to her, holding up all the while the pitcher so that she might drink more easily.
sentences.i: and rinsing her pitcher at once, she drew water from the finest spot in the spring and offered it to her, holding the pitcher up all the while so that she could drink more easily.
sentences.n: «rainçant» is «rinçant» ‘rinsing’, and «aussi-tost» is «aussitôt» ‘at once’. The witness prints «au plus belle endroit», but «endroit» ‘place, spot’ is masculine and the sense requires «au plus bel endroit» ‘at the finest spot’; whether the slip is the 1697 printer’s or the transcription’s, Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «soûtenant toûjours» is ‘holding up all the while’, with circumflexes the modern words have dropped («soutenant», «toujours»). «bût» is the imperfect subjunctive again, required by «afin que» ‘so that’. The book prints both «luy» and «lui».

sentences.t: La bonne femme ayant bu, luy dit, vous estes si belle, si bonne, & si honneste, que je ne puis m’empêcher de vous faire un don,
sentences.say: La bonne femme ayant bu, lui dit, vous êtes si belle, si bonne, et si honnête, que je ne puis m’empêcher de vous faire un don,
sentences.l: The good woman having drunk, said to her, you are so beautiful, so good, and so courteous, that I cannot keep myself from making you a gift,
sentences.i: When the good woman had drunk, she said to her, You are so beautiful, so good and so courteous that I cannot help giving you a gift,
sentences.n: «ayant bu» ‘having drunk’ is a participle clause, and «la bonne femme» is the subject both of it and of «dit». «la bonne femme» ‘the good woman’ is a homely name for an old woman of humble station. «honneste» is ‘courteous, well-mannered’, the adjective of «honnesteté», not ‘honest’. «je ne puis» is the older, more formal form of «je ne peux» ‘I cannot’, and «s’empêcher de» is ‘to keep oneself from’. «faire un don» is ‘to give a gift’, and in a fairy’s mouth the gift is a lasting endowment.

sentences.t: (car c’estoit une Fée qui avoit pris la forme d’une pauvre femme de vilage, pour voir jusqu’où iroit l’honnesteté de cette jeune fille.)
sentences.say: (car c’était une Fée qui avait pris la forme d’une pauvre femme de village, pour voir jusqu’où irait l’honnêteté de cette jeune fille.)
sentences.l: (for it was a fairy who had taken the form of a poor village woman, to see how far the courtesy of this young girl would go.)
sentences.i: (for she was a fairy who had taken the shape of a poor village woman, to see how far the young girl’s courtesy would go.)
sentences.n: The narrator’s aside, in brackets as the book prints it. «c’estoit une Fée» ‘it was a fairy’ uses «ce» where English says ‘she’. «vilage» is «village» with one l, «iroit» is the conditional of «aller» ‘would go’, and «jusqu’où» is ‘how far’, literally ‘up to where’.

sentences.t: Je vous donne pour don, poursuivit la Fée, qu’à chaque parole que vous dirés, il vous sortira de la bouche où une Fleur, où une Pierre précieuse.
sentences.say: Je vous donne pour don, poursuivit la Fée, qu’à chaque parole que vous direz, il vous sortira de la bouche où une Fleur, où une Pierre précieuse.
sentences.l: I give you as a gift, continued the Fairy, that at each word that you will say, there will come out to you from the mouth either a flower or a precious stone.
sentences.i: This is the gift I give you, the Fairy went on: at every word you speak, a flower or a precious stone shall come out of your mouth.
sentences.n: «donner pour don» ‘to give as a gift’ is the fairies’ formula for bestowing, and «il vous sortira de la bouche» is ‘there will come out of your mouth’, with «vous» where English says ‘your’. The witness prints «où … où», which would be ‘where … where’; the sense requires «ou … ou» ‘either … or’, as in the elder sister’s gift, and Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «dirés» is an older spelling of «direz» ‘you will say’. «poursuivit» ‘continued’ is the passé simple of «poursuivre».

sentences.t: Lorsque cette belle fille arriva au logis, sa mere la gronda de revenir si tard de la fontaine.
sentences.say: Lorsque cette belle fille arriva au logis, sa mère la gronda de revenir si tard de la fontaine.
sentences.l: When this beautiful girl arrived at the house, her mother scolded her for coming back so late from the spring.
sentences.i: When the beautiful girl reached home, her mother scolded her for coming back so late from the spring.
sentences.n: «arriva» and «gronda» are passé simple, one event after the other. «gronder quelqu’un de» with an infinitive is ‘to scold someone for’ doing something.

sentences.t: Je vous demande pardon, ma mere, dit cette pauvre fille, d’avoir tardé si long-temps,
sentences.say: Je vous demande pardon, ma mère, dit cette pauvre fille, d’avoir tardé si longtemps,
sentences.l: I ask you pardon, my mother, said this poor girl, for having delayed so long,
sentences.i: I beg your pardon, Mother, said the poor girl, for being so long,
sentences.n: The girl says «vous» to her mother, the ordinary respectful form from a child to a parent, and the mother will say «vous» to her elder daughter too; all of it is ‘you’ in the English. «tarder» is ‘to be late, to linger’, and «long-temps» is «longtemps», still printed as two words joined by a hyphen.

sentences.t: & en disant ces mots il luy sortit de la bouche deux Roses, deux Perles, & deux gros Diamants.
sentences.say: et en disant ces mots il lui sortit de la bouche deux Roses, deux Perles, et deux gros Diamants.
sentences.l: and in saying these words there came out to her from the mouth two roses, two pearls, and two big diamonds.
sentences.i: and as she said these words, two roses, two pearls and two large diamonds came out of her mouth.
sentences.n: «il luy sortit de la bouche» is the gift come true, in the passé simple: ‘there came out of her mouth’. The Fairy promised a flower or a stone, and roses, pearls and diamonds are what come; the capitals on the nouns are the 1697 printer’s. «en disant» ‘in saying, while saying’ is the gerund of «dire».

sentences.t: Que voy je là, dit sa mere toute estonnée, je crois qu’il luy sort de la bouche des Perles & des Diamants, d’où vient cela, ma fille,
sentences.say: Que vois je là, dit sa mère toute étonnée, je crois qu’il lui sort de la bouche des Perles et des Diamants, d’où vient cela, ma fille,
sentences.l: What do I see there, said her mother all astonished, I believe that there comes out to her from the mouth pearls and diamonds, where does that come from, my daughter,
sentences.i: What is this I see? said her mother, thunderstruck. I do believe pearls and diamonds are coming out of her mouth! Where does this come from, my daughter?
sentences.n: «voy je» is an older spelling of «vois-je» ‘do I see’, printed without the hyphen, and the witness sets no question marks in the speech; the idiomatic line supplies them. «estonnée» is «étonnée», in 1697 a stronger word than today’s ‘surprised’: ‘astounded, thunderstruck’. «il luy sort de la bouche» is the gift’s formula again, now in the present. «ma fille» ‘my daughter’: the mother is speaking to the younger girl.

sentences.t: (ce fut là la premiere fois qu’elle l’appela sa fille.)
sentences.say: (ce fut là la première fois qu’elle l’appela sa fille.)
sentences.l: (this was the first time that she called her her daughter.)
sentences.i: (it was the first time she had ever called her her daughter.)
sentences.n: The narrator’s second aside. «ce fut là» ‘that was’ is the passé simple, with «là» adding weight, and «premiere» is «première» without its accent. The dry remark lets the reader see the mother’s affection arrive with the diamonds.

sentences.t: La pauvre enfant luy raconta naïvement tout ce qui luy estoit arrivé, non sans jetter une infinité de Diamants.
sentences.say: La pauvre enfant lui raconta naïvement tout ce qui lui était arrivé, non sans jeter une infinité de Diamants.
sentences.l: The poor child told her artlessly all that had happened to her, not without throwing an infinity of diamonds.
sentences.i: The poor child told her plainly all that had happened to her, not without casting out countless diamonds.
sentences.n: «naïvement» is ‘artlessly, openly, without guile’, from the old sense of «naïf» ‘natural, unaffected’, not ‘foolishly’. «jetter» is the 1697 spelling of «jeter» ‘to throw, cast’, and «une infinité de» ‘an infinity of’ is ‘countless’. In «la pauvre enfant» the word «enfant» takes the feminine article because the child is a girl.

sentences.t: Vrayment, dit la mere, il faut que j’y envoye ma fille, tenez Fanchon, voyez ce qui sort de la bouche de vôtre sœur quand elle parle, ne seriez vous pas bien aise d’avor le même don,
sentences.say: Vraiment, dit la mère, il faut que j’y envoie ma fille, tenez Fanchon, voyez ce qui sort de la bouche de vôtre sœur quand elle parle, ne seriez vous pas bien aise d’avoir le même don,
sentences.l: Truly, said the mother, it is needful that I send my daughter there, here Fanchon, see what comes out of the mouth of your sister when she speaks, would you not be very glad to have the same gift,
sentences.i: Truly, said the mother, I must send my daughter there. Here, Fanchon, look what comes out of your sister’s mouth when she speaks! Would you not be very glad to have the same gift?
sentences.n: «Vrayment» is «vraiment» ‘truly’, «envoye» is «envoie», and «il faut que» ‘it is needful that’ takes the present subjunctive. «ma fille» now means the elder: a moment ago the mother gave the name to the younger for the first time, and here it goes back where it was. «Fanchon» is a familiar pet form of «Françoise», and the elder is the only one of the sisters the tale names. «tenez», literally ‘hold’, is ‘here, look’; «vôtre» is «votre», and «bien aise» is ‘very glad’. The witness prints «d’avor», which is not a word: the sense requires «d’avoir» ‘to have’, and Lectorium prints its witness unaltered.

sentences.t: vous n’avez qu’à aller puiser de l’eau à la fontaine, & quand une pauvre femme vous demandera à boire, luy en donner bien honnestement.
sentences.say: vous n’avez qu’à aller puiser de l’eau à la fontaine, et quand une pauvre femme vous demandera à boire, lui en donner bien honnêtement.
sentences.l: you have only to go draw water at the spring, and when a poor woman asks you for a drink, to give her some very courteously.
sentences.i: You have only to go and draw water at the spring, and when a poor woman asks you for a drink, give her some, very civilly.
sentences.n: «n’avoir qu’à» with an infinitive is ‘to have only to’, and both «aller puiser» and «luy en donner» hang on it. French puts the future «demandera» ‘will ask’ after «quand» where English uses the present. «en» is ‘some (of it)’, the water, and «bien honnestement» is ‘very courteously’.

sentences.t: Il me feroit beau voir, répondit la brutale, aller à la fontaine : Je veux que vous y alliez, reprit la mere, & toute à l’heure.
sentences.say: Il me ferait beau voir, répondit la brutale, aller à la fontaine : Je veux que vous y alliez, reprit la mère, et toute à l’heure.
sentences.l: It would be fine to see me, answered the brutish one, go to the spring: I want you to go there, returned the mother, and this very moment.
sentences.i: A fine sight I would be, answered the boorish girl, going to the spring! I want you to go there, said the mother, and this minute.
sentences.n: «Il me feroit beau voir» is sarcasm: «il feroit beau voir» ‘it would be a fine thing to see’ is said of something one will not stand for, and «me» makes the girl herself the spectacle; «feroit» is «ferait». «brutal» in 1697 is ‘like a brute beast’: coarse, boorish, rough in manner and temper; here the word fixes on the girl’s rudeness, and «la brutale» ‘the brutish one’ is the tale’s name for the elder in the scenes that follow. «Je veux que vous y alliez» takes the present subjunctive. «toute à l’heure» (modern «tout à l’heure») then meant ‘at once, this very moment’, where today it means ‘in a little while’ or ‘a little while ago’.

sentences.t: Elle y alla, mais toûjours en grondant.
sentences.say: Elle y alla, mais toujours en grondant.
sentences.l: She went there, but always grumbling.
sentences.i: She went, but grumbling all the way.
sentences.n: «alla» is the passé simple of «aller», and «y» is ‘there’. «gronder» here is ‘to grumble’, where earlier it was the mother’s ‘scolding’; «en grondant» ‘in grumbling’ is the gerund, and «toûjours» ‘always’ has the sense ‘all the while’.

sentences.t: Elle prit le plus beau Flacon d’argent qui fut dans le logis.
sentences.l: She took the most beautiful silver flask that was in the house.
sentences.i: She took the finest silver flask in the house.
sentences.n: A «flacon» is a flask or bottle with a stopper, and a silver one is a piece of fine household plate, hardly a vessel for drawing water. After a superlative French expects the subjunctive «qui fût», and the witness’s «fut» without the circumflex is probably that subjunctive, since the book’s accents are irregular.

sentences.t: Elle ne fut pas plustost arrivée à la fontaine qu’elle vit sortir du bois une Dame magnifiquement vestuë qui vint luy demander à boire,
sentences.say: Elle ne fut pas plutôt arrivée à la fontaine qu’elle vit sortir du bois une Dame magnifiquement vêtue qui vint lui demander à boire,
sentences.l: She was not sooner arrived at the spring than she saw come out of the wood a lady magnificently dressed who came to ask her for a drink,
sentences.i: No sooner had she reached the spring than she saw a magnificently dressed lady come out of the wood, who came up and asked her for a drink.
sentences.n: «ne … pas plustost … que» is ‘no sooner … than’, with «plustost» the 1697 spelling of «plus tôt». «arriver» forms its past with «estre» ‘to be’, as English once said ‘she was arrived’. «vestuë» is «vêtue» ‘dressed’, in the old spelling with s and diaeresis. «voir sortir» is ‘to see come out’, and a «Dame» ‘lady’ was a woman of rank.

sentences.t: c’estoit la même Fée qui avoit apparu à sa sœur, mais qui avoit pris l’air & les habits d’une Princesse, pour voir jusqu’où iroit la malhonnesteté de cette fille.
sentences.say: c’était la même Fée qui avait apparu à sa sœur, mais qui avait pris l’air et les habits d’une Princesse, pour voir jusqu’où irait la malhonnêteté de cette fille.
sentences.l: it was the same fairy who had appeared to her sister, but who had taken the air and the clothes of a princess, to see how far the discourtesy of this girl would go.
sentences.i: It was the same fairy who had appeared to her sister, but she had taken on the bearing and the dress of a princess, to see how far this girl’s rudeness would go.
sentences.n: The aside repeats the first one almost word for word, «pour voir jusqu’où iroit» ‘to see how far would go’, with «malhonnesteté» ‘discourtesy, rudeness’ in place of «honnesteté»; modern «malhonnêteté» mostly means ‘dishonesty’, a sense it does not have here. «l’air» is ‘bearing, manner’, and «habits» is ‘clothes’.

sentences.t: Est-ce que je suis icy venuë, luy dit cette brutale orgueileuse, pour vous donner à boire, justement j’ai apporté un Flacon d’argent tout exprés pour donner à boire à Madame ?
sentences.say: Est-ce que je suis ici venue, lui dit cette brutale orgueilleuse, pour vous donner à boire, justement j’ai apporté un Flacon d’argent tout exprès pour donner à boire à Madame ?
sentences.l: Is it that I am come here, said to her this proud brutish one, to give you [something] to drink, just so, I have brought a silver flask expressly to give Madame [something] to drink?
sentences.i: Did I come here, the proud, boorish girl said to her, to give you a drink? To be sure, I brought a silver flask on purpose to give Madame a drink!
sentences.n: Scorn from start to finish. «Est-ce que je suis icy venuë … pour» ‘is it that I have come here … to’ is a question expecting the answer no, and «justement … tout exprés» ‘just so … expressly’ is heavy irony. Speaking of a stranger as «Madame» in the third person is the deferential form a servant would use, turned here into a sneer. «icy» is «ici», «venuë» «venue», «exprés» «exprès», and «orgueileuse» is printed with one l, where the first paragraph had «orgueilleuses». The literal line supplies [something] after ‘to give’ both times.

sentences.t: J’en suis d’avis, beuvez à même si vous voulez.
sentences.say: J’en suis d’avis, buvez à même si vous voulez.
sentences.l: I am of that opinion, drink straight [from it] if you want.
sentences.i: A fine idea! Drink straight from the spring if you like.
sentences.n: «J’en suis d’avis» is literally ‘I am of that opinion’; here it is sarcastic, something like ‘a fine idea!’, though its exact tone is hard to pin down. «beuvez» is an older form of «buvez» ‘drink’, and «boire à même» is ‘to drink straight from’ the source, without cup or flask; the literal line supplies [from it].

sentences.t: Vous n’estes guere honneste, reprit la Fée, sans se mettre en colere,
sentences.say: Vous n’êtes guère honnête, reprit la Fée, sans se mettre en colère,
sentences.l: You are hardly courteous, returned the fairy, without putting herself in anger,
sentences.i: You are not very courteous, said the fairy, without growing angry.
sentences.n: «ne … guere» (modern «guère») is ‘hardly, not much’. «reprit», the passé simple of «reprendre», is ‘took up again, replied’. «se mettre en colere» is ‘to get angry’, «colere» being «colère» without its accent. The fairy keeps her temper, and says «vous» to this girl as she did to the sister.

sentences.t: & bien, puisque vous estes si peu obligeante, je vous donne pour don, qu’à chaque parole que vous direz, il vous sortira de la bouche ou un serpent ou un crapau.
sentences.say: et bien, puisque vous êtes si peu obligeante, je vous donne pour don, qu’à chaque parole que vous direz, il vous sortira de la bouche ou un serpent ou un crapaud.
sentences.l: Well, since you are so little obliging, I give you as a gift that at each word that you will say, there will come out to you from the mouth either a snake or a toad.
sentences.i: Well, since you are so unwilling to oblige, this is the gift I give you: at every word you speak, a snake or a toad shall come out of your mouth.
sentences.n: The Fairy gives the elder sister the younger’s formula word for word, with the flower and the stone turned into «un serpent» ‘a snake’ and «un crapau» ‘a toad’ («crapau» is the 1697 spelling of «crapaud»). When the girl first speaks, what comes out is «deux viperes» ‘two vipers’, a particular kind of snake. «& bien» here is «eh bien» ‘well, well then’, which the period often wrote «et bien», and so could print with the sign «&»; the literal line gives ‘Well’, not ‘and well’. «obligeante» is ‘obliging, ready to do a kindness’.

sentences.t: D’abord que sa mere l’aperçeut, elle luy cria, Hé bien ma fille ! Hé bien, ma mere, luy répondit la brutale, en jettant deux viperes, & deux crapaux,
sentences.say: D’abord que sa mère l’aperçut, elle lui cria, Hé bien ma fille ! Hé bien, ma mère, lui répondit la brutale, en jetant deux vipères, et deux crapauds,
sentences.l: As soon as her mother caught sight of her, she cried to her, Well, my daughter! Well, my mother, the brutish one answered her, throwing two vipers, and two toads,
sentences.i: As soon as her mother caught sight of her, she called out, Well, daughter? Well, Mother, answered the boorish girl, casting out two vipers and two toads.
sentences.n: «en jettant» ‘(while) throwing’ is the gerund of «jetter» (modern «jeter»), the verb already used of the younger sister, who tells her story «non sans jetter une infinité de Diamants»; the English says ‘casting out’ in both places. «viperes» and «crapaux» are 1697 spellings of «vipères» and «crapauds». «D’abord que» is an older ‘as soon as’ (modern «dès que»), and «aperçeut» is «aperçut» ‘caught sight of’, passé simple, printed with an extra e. «Hé bien» is the same «eh bien» as the fairy’s «& bien», spelled another way; the daughter answers her mother’s eager question with the mother’s own two words.

sentences.t: O ! Ciel, s’écria la mere, que vois-je là, c’est sa sœur qui en est cause, elle me le payera ;
sentences.say: Ô ! Ciel, s’écria la mère, que vois-je là, c’est sa sœur qui en est cause, elle me le payera ;
sentences.l: O! Heaven, cried the mother, what do I see there, it is her sister who is the cause of it, she will pay me for it;
sentences.i: Heavens! cried the mother. What is this I see? It is her sister’s doing, and she shall pay me for it!
sentences.n: «O Ciel» ‘O Heaven’ is a cry of dismay; «Ciel» is ‘heaven, the sky’. «c’est sa sœur qui en est cause» ‘it is her sister who is the cause of it’ puts the blame first, and «sa sœur» is the younger girl, named from the elder’s side. «elle me le payera» ‘she will pay me for it’ is a threat; «payera» is a form of the future still in use beside «paiera».

sentences.t: & aussi-tost elle courut pour la battre.
sentences.say: et aussitôt elle courut pour la battre.
sentences.l: and at once she ran to beat her.
sentences.i: And at once she ran to give her a beating.
sentences.n: «courut» is the passé simple of «courir» ‘to run’, and «la» ‘her’ is the younger daughter, whom the mother means to beat.

sentences.t: La pauvre enfant s’enfuit, & alla se sauver dans la Forest prochaine.
sentences.say: La pauvre enfant s’enfuit, et alla se sauver dans la Forêt prochaine.
sentences.l: The poor child fled, and went to save herself in the nearby forest.
sentences.i: The poor child fled and took refuge in the nearby forest.
sentences.n: «s’enfuit» ‘fled’ and «alla» ‘went’ are passé simple. «se sauver» is ‘to escape, to take refuge’, and «prochaine» here is ‘nearest, nearby’, not ‘next’ in time. «Forest» is «forêt», the s again standing where the modern word has a circumflex.

sentences.t: Le fils du Roi qui revenoit de la chasse, la rencontra, & la voyant si belle, luy demanda ce qu’elle faisoit là toute seule & ce qu’elle avoit à pleurer.
sentences.say: Le fils du Roi qui revenait de la chasse, la rencontra, et la voyant si belle, lui demanda ce qu’elle faisait là toute seule et ce qu’elle avait à pleurer.
sentences.l: The son of the King, who was coming back from the hunt, met her, and seeing her so beautiful, asked her what she was doing there all alone and what she had to weep about.
sentences.i: The King’s son, returning from the hunt, came upon her, and seeing how beautiful she was, asked her what she was doing there all alone and why she was weeping.
sentences.n: «le fils du Roi» ‘the son of the King’ is the tale’s name for the prince. Hunting was the great pastime of kings and princes. «revenoit» ‘was coming back’ is the imperfect, the background, and «rencontra» ‘met’ the passé simple, the event. «ce qu’elle avoit à pleurer» is ‘what she had to weep for’.

sentences.t: Helas ! Monsieur, c’est ma mere qui m’a chassée du logis.
sentences.say: Hélas ! Monsieur, c’est ma mère qui m’a chassée du logis.
sentences.l: Alas! Sir, it is my mother who has driven me out of the house.
sentences.i: Alas, sir, my mother has driven me from home.
sentences.n: «Helas» is «hélas» ‘alas’, and «Monsieur» ‘sir’ is the courteous address to a gentleman. «chasser» is ‘to drive out’, and the same verb gives «la chasse» ‘the hunt’ from which the prince was returning. «chassée» agrees with «m’» because the one driven out is a girl.

sentences.t: Le fils du Roi qui vit sortir de sa bouche cinq ou six Perles, & autant de Diamants, la pria de luy dire d’où cela luy venoit.
sentences.say: Le fils du Roi qui vit sortir de sa bouche cinq ou six Perles, et autant de Diamants, la pria de lui dire d’où cela lui venait.
sentences.l: The son of the King, who saw come out of her mouth five or six pearls, and as many diamonds, begged her to tell him where that came to her from.
sentences.i: The King’s son, seeing five or six pearls and as many diamonds come out of her mouth, begged her to tell him how this had come to her.
sentences.n: «vit» ‘saw’ is the passé simple of «voir», and «voir sortir» ‘to see come out’ is the same construction as in the elder sister’s scene. «autant de» is ‘as many’. «prier» is ‘to beg, ask’, not only ‘to pray’, and «d’où cela luy venoit» is ‘where that came to her from’.

sentences.t: Elle luy conta toute son avanture.
sentences.say: Elle lui conta toute son aventure.
sentences.l: She told him all her adventure.
sentences.i: She told him everything that had happened to her.
sentences.n: «conta» is the passé simple of «conter» ‘to tell’, the verb behind «conte» ‘tale’. «avanture» is the 1697 spelling of «aventure», in the older sense ‘what befell her’, not a daring exploit.

sentences.t: Le fils du Roi en devint amoureux, & considerant qu’un tel don valoit mieux que tout ce qu’on pouvoit donner en mariage à une autre, l’emmena au Palais du Roi son pere, où il l’épousa.
sentences.say: Le fils du Roi en devint amoureux, et considérant qu’un tel don valait mieux que tout ce qu’on pouvait donner en mariage à une autre, l’emmena au Palais du Roi son père, où il l’épousa.
sentences.l: The son of the King became in love with her, and considering that such a gift was worth more than all that one could give in marriage to another, took her to the palace of the King his father, where he married her.
sentences.i: The King’s son fell in love with her, and judging that such a gift was worth more than any dowry another bride could bring, took her to the palace of the King his father, and there he married her.
sentences.n: «en devint amoureux» is ‘fell in love with her’, literally ‘of her became in love’, with «en» standing for ‘of her’. «ce qu’on pouvoit donner en mariage» is a dowry, the money and goods a bride’s family settled on her at marriage; the prince reckons the girl’s gift worth more than any other bride’s portion. «valoit mieux» is ‘was worth more’, and «considerant» is «considérant» without its accent.

sentences.t: Pour sa sœur elle se fit tant haïr, que sa propre mere la chassa de chez elle ;
sentences.say: Pour sa sœur elle se fit tant haïr, que sa propre mère la chassa de chez elle ;
sentences.l: As for her sister, she made herself so hated, that her own mother drove her out of her home;
sentences.i: As for her sister, she made herself so hated that her own mother drove her from the house;
sentences.n: «Pour» at the head of a sentence is ‘as for’. «se faire haïr» is ‘to make oneself hated’, «faire» with an infinitive again. «chasser» ‘to drive out’ is the verb the younger used of her own treatment, and now it falls on the elder.

sentences.t: & la malheureuse aprés avoir bien couru sans trouver personne qui voulut la recevoir, alla mourir au coin d’un bois.
sentences.say: et la malheureuse après avoir bien couru sans trouver personne qui voulut la recevoir, alla mourir au coin d’un bois.
sentences.l: and the unhappy one, after having run about a great deal without finding anyone who would take her in, went to die at the corner of a wood.
sentences.i: and the wretched girl, after wandering far and wide without finding anyone willing to take her in, went off and died in a corner of a wood.
sentences.n: «la malheureuse» is ‘the unhappy one, the wretch’, and «aprés» is «après», with the accent the other way. «avoir bien couru» ‘to have run a good deal’ is ‘to have roamed far’, and «recevoir» here is ‘to take in, give shelter’. After «sans … personne» ‘without … anyone’ French expects the subjunctive «voulût»; the witness prints «voulut», most likely that form without its circumflex, since the book’s accents are irregular. «au coin d’un bois» ‘at the corner of a wood’ is some lonely, out-of-the-way spot, and «alla mourir» ‘went to die’ is the tale’s blunt last word on her.

sentences.t: MORALITÉ
sentences.l: MORAL
sentences.n: «MORALITÉ» is ‘moral’. The verses belong to the tale as the book prints it, and this tale closes with two morals, the second headed «Autre Moralité».

sentences.t:
Les Diamans et les Pistoles
Peuvent beaucoup sur les esprits ;
Cependant les douces paroles
Ont encor plus de force, et sont d’un plus grand prix.
sentences.say:
Les Diamants et les Pistoles,
Peuvent beaucoup sur les esprits ;
Cependant les douces paroles,
Ont encor plus de force, et sont d’un plus grand prix.
sentences.l:
The diamonds and the pistoles
Can do much upon minds;
Nevertheless the sweet words
Have still more force, and are of a greater price.
sentences.i:
Diamonds and gold coins
have great sway over people’s minds;
yet gentle words
have greater force still, and are worth more.
sentences.n: «Diamans» is the tale’s «Diamants» without the t, another spelling of the time. A «pistole» was a gold coin, first Spanish, long current in France and a byword for money. «pouvoir beaucoup sur» is ‘to have great power over’, and «esprits» here is ‘minds’. «douces paroles» ‘gentle words’ takes up «parole», the word of the gifts: at each «parole» a flower or a stone, a snake or a toad. «encor» is a spelling of «encore» ‘still’ that poets used when the metre wanted a syllable fewer, and «prix» is ‘worth, value’ as well as ‘price’.

sentences.t: Autre Moralité
sentences.l: ANOTHER MORAL
sentences.n: «Autre» is ‘other, another’. A second moral, as four other tales in the book also have; the witness prints this heading with capitals only on its initials, where the first heading stands in full capitals.

sentences.t:
L’onnesteté couste des soins,
Et veut un peu de complaisance,
Mais tost ou tard elle a sa récompense,
Et souvent dans le temps qu’on y pense le moins.
sentences.say:
L’honnêteté coûte des soins,
Et veut un peu de complaisance,
Mais tôt ou tard elle a sa récompense,
Et souvent dans le temps qu’on y pense le moins.
sentences.l:
Courtesy costs pains,
And wants a little complaisance,
But soon or late it has its reward,
And often in the time that one thinks of it the least.
sentences.i:
Courtesy takes some trouble
and asks a little willingness to please,
but sooner or later it has its reward,
and often just when one least expects it.
sentences.n: The witness prints «L’onnesteté», without the h of «honnesteté» that the tale itself uses; the sense is plainly the same word, ‘courtesy’, and whether the missing h is the 1697 printer’s or the transcription’s, Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «couste» is «coûte» and «tost» is «tôt». «soins» is ‘pains, trouble, careful effort’, «veut» is ‘wants’ in the old sense ‘requires’, and «complaisance» is the readiness to please others and fall in with their wishes, without the smugness of English ‘complacency’. «dans le temps qu’on y pense le moins» is ‘at the time when one least thinks of it’, with «y» ‘of it’.
